title: Listening to Mozart won’t make you, or your baby, smarter
body: In 1993 a small study found that college students who listened to a Mozart sonata scored slightly better on spatial reasoning tasks for about 15 minutes afterwards. Media reports turned this into ‘Mozart makes babies smarter’, and the governor of Georgia even proposed giving every newborn a classical music CD. Later attempts to replicate the result were mixed, and reviews found little or no lasting effect on intelligence.

slides.question: How many students took part in the original 1993 Mozart study?
slides.explanation: Just 36 college students listened to a Mozart sonata, then did spatial puzzles such as paper folding. No babies, and no claims about general intelligence.

slides.heading: What was actually tested
slides.text: 36 college students, one Mozart sonata for two pianos, then spatial puzzles such as paper folding. No babies, and no claims about general intelligence.

slides.heading: A likely explanation
slides.text: Music or stories people enjoy can briefly lift mood and alertness, which nudges test scores. Similar bumps have been found with music other than Mozart.

slides.heading: What may help
slides.text: Actually learning an instrument is linked to some cognitive benefits, though how large they are, and whether they carry over to other skills, is still debated.
